737-600: The 737-600 has the shortest fuselage of the Next Generation 737 family, giving it a notably stubby appearance.
It usually has only about three to four cabin windows in front of the wing, fewer than on longer 737 variants.
Behind the wing, it also has a shorter run of cabin windows than the 737-700, 737-800, or 737-900.
The aircraft keeps the standard 737 wing size, so the wings look relatively large compared with its short body.
Its proportions make the plane appear compact, with a short fuselage balanced by full-size wings and tail surfaces.
The tail and vertical fin look slightly oversized relative to the body because the fuselage is so short.
The 737-600 shares the rounded Next Generation 737 nose shape rather than the flatter look of earlier classics.
It normally uses CFM56-7B engines, which have the characteristic flattened bottom nacelles of 737 jet engines.
Compared with a 737-700, the distance between the front passenger door and the wing is visibly shorter.
Compared with a 737-800, the 737-600 looks dramatically shorter both ahead of and behind the wing.
The overwing exit arrangement matches a small Next Generation 737, helping separate it from older 737 variants.
Its landing gear stance is the familiar low-slung 737 posture, but on a very short fuselage.
The aircraft often looks like a shrunken 737-700, with nearly the same wing and tail on a shorter tube.
The wingtip style may be blended winglets or no winglets, but the short fuselage remains the key identifier.
The rear fuselage from the wing to the tail is especially abbreviated compared with other modern 737s.
The cabin door spacing looks tight because the nose door and tail door are closer together than on larger 737s.
The plane’s overall silhouette is compact and balanced, lacking the stretched look of the 737-800 and 737-900.
From the side, the wing sits on a body that seems too short for it, which is a strong clue it is a 737-600.
The 737-600 does not have the very long cabin of the 737-900 or the medium-length look of the 737-700.
If it looks like a Next Generation 737 but unusually short and stocky, it is likely a 737-600.
707-320: The 707-320 has a noticeably longer fuselage than the early 707 variants.
Its wingspan is greater than that of the 707-120, giving it a broader overall stance.
The wing often shows a distinct span extension outboard of the inboard engines.
It has four turbojet or low-bypass turbofan engines mounted singly under the wings.
The vertical tail is tall and swept, with the classic narrow 707 fin shape.
The horizontal stabilizer is mounted low on the tail rather than in a T-tail arrangement.
The fuselage is a classic narrow-body tube with a single aisle cabin cross section.
The nose profile is rounded and slightly pointed, typical of early Boeing jetliners.
The cockpit windshield has the characteristic angular multi-pane 707 window arrangement.
The engine nacelles sit relatively close to the wing compared with later widebody designs.
The landing gear is a conventional tricycle arrangement with two main gear assemblies under the wings.
The main landing gear retracts into prominent fairings at the wing root area.
The aircraft has a long, straight cabin window row running much of the fuselage length.
The tailcone is slender and tapers neatly behind the rear fuselage.
Compared with shorter 707s, the 707-320 has more space visible between the wing and the tail.
The wings are swept back strongly, giving the aircraft a distinctly 1950s jetliner look.
The inboard and outboard engines are evenly spaced along each wing in a simple four-engine layout.
The fuselage usually appears more stretched ahead of and behind the wing than on the 707-120.
Many 707-320s have a taller-fin appearance than the earliest production 707 versions.
The overall silhouette combines a long narrow fuselage, swept wings, and four underwing engines in a proportion distinctive to the 707-320.
737-400: The 737-400 has the classic 737 body shape but with a noticeably longer fuselage than a 737-300.
It usually has two overwing exit hatches on each side instead of just one per side.
The airplane has the low-slung stance typical of early 737 generations, with engines sitting close to the ground.
Its engines are the older CFM56 style with flattened bottoms rather than fully round nacelles.
The nose has the pointed, traditional 737 profile rather than the more modern 737NG look.
The cockpit windows have the angular classic 737 shape, including the distinctive eyebrow-window-era styling on some aircraft.
The vertical tail is the original classic 737 fin shape, without the revised proportions seen on later versions.
The wing is the shorter classic 737 wing, not the larger redesigned wing of the Next Generation models.
The main landing gear does not have gear doors covering the wheels after retraction, which is typical of the 737 family.
Compared with a 737-500, the 737-400 looks much longer and more stretched in side view.
Compared with a 737-300, the 737-400’s longer cabin makes the spacing of doors and windows look more extended.
The aircraft often has a single main passenger door at the front and rear, plus overwing exits in the middle.
The tail cone is the classic short 737 style and lacks the updated look of newer generations.
The engine nacelles sit slightly ahead of the wing leading edge and appear somewhat squashed underneath.
The fuselage length gives the airplane a slim, elongated appearance compared with other classic 737 variants.
The winglets are usually absent, since most 737-400s were built without them.
If winglets are present, they are typically retrofit blended winglets rather than the split style seen on newer 737s.
The airplane has the overall visual combination of a stretched classic 737 fuselage with old-style engines.
The cabin window line runs a long distance between the front and rear doors, emphasizing the stretched body.
The 737-400 is best recognized as a classic-series 737 with flattened-bottom engines and two overwing exits per side.
737-300: The 737-300 has the classic narrow 737 fuselage with engines mounted low under each wing.
It uses older CFM56 turbofan nacelles with a flattened bottom that gives the engines a hamster pouch look.
The nose is the traditional early 737 shape rather than the more sculpted nose seen on newer models.
It has the short to medium fuselage length that is longer than a 737-200 but clearly shorter than a 737-400.
The cockpit windows have the classic angular 737 appearance without the newer style window surrounds.
The wing tips are usually simple and straight without the tall blended winglets common on later aircraft.
The main landing gear sits close to the fuselage because the 737-300 has relatively low ground clearance.
The tail cone is the older slim style used on Classic 737 models.
The vertical tail is proportioned like the 737 Classic family and lacks the revised look of the Next Generation series.
The airplane typically has two overwing exit doors, one on each side, which helps separate it from some smaller variants.
The engine nacelles sit noticeably ahead of the wing leading edge when viewed from the side.
The fan intakes look slightly squashed at the bottom because the nacelles were reshaped to fit the low airframe.
The fuselage usually shows the 737 Classic arrangement of passenger windows and doors rather than the MAX layout.
The wings are relatively short and simple in planform compared with later 737 generations.
The tail height and overall proportions give it a compact, balanced look typical of the 737-300.
It lacks the eyebrow windows above the cockpit on most aircraft because many were built without them or had them removed.
The engine exhaust and nacelle shape are more rounded and older-looking than those on NG and MAX models.
The airplane has the 737 Classic combination of a traditional tail, flattened nacelles, and low stance on the ramp.
From the side, the 737-300 looks like a mid-length Classic with one overwing exit and no stretched rear fuselage.
Its overall appearance matches the 737 Classic family, especially the distinctive flattened CFM56 engine nacelles and modest fuselage length.
727-200: A Boeing 727-200 has three jet engines, with one engine mounted on each side of the rear fuselage and a third engine fed by a central S-duct at the base of the tail.
The aircraft uses a T-tail, with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on top of the vertical fin.
Its fuselage is noticeably longer than the 727-100, giving it a stretched appearance with more cabin windows.
The nose is pointed and classic in shape, typical of early Boeing narrow-body airliners.
The wings are swept back and carry large trailing-edge flaps for low-speed performance.
The main landing gear retracts into pods and bays near the lower fuselage rather than into the wings like many later jets.
The rear fuselage looks busy and distinctive because all three engines are clustered at the tail.
The center engine intake appears as an oval opening just ahead of the vertical fin root.
From the side, the tail section looks tall and heavy because of the combination of the T-tail and central intake.
The 727-200 usually has more overwing and forward cabin windows than the shorter 727-100, making the stretch visible in profile.
The aircraft has a narrow-body fuselage with a single aisle, giving it a slim cylindrical cross-section.
Its cockpit windshield has an older angular style that differs from more modern smoothly blended airliners.
The engine nacelles on the sides of the rear fuselage sit close to the body instead of hanging under the wings.
The wing-mounted gear fairings and underside contours help give the airplane a distinctly 1960s trijet look.
A ventral airstair is often associated with the type, built into the rear fuselage underside on many aircraft.
The vertical tail is relatively tall and broad to support the high-mounted horizontal stabilizer and center engine ducting.
The trailing edge of the wing includes multiple flap segments, which are prominent when deployed.
The airplane lacks wingtip devices in its original form, so the wing tips appear clean and simple.
The rear-mounted engines leave the wings visually uncluttered, with no engine nacelles beneath them.
Compared with twinjets, the 727-200 is easy to spot by its unmistakable trijet layout and stretched fuselage.
737-500: The Boeing 737-500 is one of the shortest members of the 737 Classic family, giving it a noticeably stubby fuselage.
It has the classic 737 rounded nose shape rather than the sharper nose seen on newer Boeing narrowbodies.
The aircraft uses CFM56 engines with flattened bottoms on the nacelles because of the 737’s low ground clearance.
Its engine nacelles are less rounded and more compact than those on the newer 737 Next Generation models.
The main landing gear does not have full gear doors, leaving the wheels partly exposed when retracted.
It has a conventional tail cone shape typical of the 737 Classic series.
The vertical tail is proportioned like other 737 Classics and is less swept and refined than on later variants.
The wing is the original 737 wing design without the larger updated trailing edge of the NG series.
Most 737-500s were built without winglets, so a clean wingtip is a common identifying feature.
If winglets are present, they are usually aftermarket blended winglets rather than the split scimitar type.
The fuselage is shorter than a 737-300 and much shorter than a 737-400, which is often the easiest comparison point.
It typically has fewer passenger windows along the cabin because of its shorter body length.
The overwing exit arrangement matches the small Classic fuselage layout, helping separate it from longer variants.
The cockpit windshield shape is the older 737 style shared with all Classic models.
It lacks the reshaped tailcone and more modern rear fuselage details seen on the 737 Next Generation family.
The aircraft sits relatively low to the ground, which is especially obvious when viewed from the side.
The engines appear close to the wing and ground, reinforcing the low-slung look of the 737 Classic.
The overall profile looks compact, with a short fuselage ahead of and behind the wing.
Compared with the 737-200, it has larger high-bypass turbofan engines instead of the older skinny turbojets.
Compared with newer 737 variants, it combines a short fuselage with Classic-era flat-bottom engine nacelles and usually no winglets.
737-700: The 737-700 is a short-bodied member of the Next Generation 737 family with a noticeably shorter fuselage than the 737-800.
It has the classic 737 nose shape and cockpit windows used on the 737 Next Generation series.
The aircraft usually has one overwing exit on each side, unlike longer 737 variants that often have more exit doors or additional overwing exits.
Its proportions look compact, with a relatively short cabin sitting on the same low-slung landing gear as other 737s.
The wings are the Next Generation style, broader and more refined than those on the older 737 Classic models.
Many 737-700s are fitted with blended winglets or split scimitar winglets, though some may appear without winglets.
The engine nacelles are the flattened-bottom CFM56 type used on Next Generation 737s.
The main landing gear does not have the taller stance seen on newer 737 MAX aircraft.
The tailcone is the standard 737 NG shape and lacks any dramatic extension or unusual rear fuselage profile.
Compared with the 737-600, the 737-700 is visibly longer while keeping the same general fuselage cross section.
Compared with the 737-800, the 737-700 has fewer passenger windows because of its shorter fuselage.
The distance between the wing and the rear door appears shorter on a 737-700 than on a 737-800.
The distance from the nose to the wing is also shorter than on the stretched 737-800 and 737-900.
It has two main cabin doors per side in the standard layout, plus a single overwing exit per side.
The vertical tail is the same general size and shape as other 737 NG variants, which makes the shorter fuselage stand out.
The aircraft sits close to the ground, giving it the familiar low-profile 737 appearance.
Its overall look is balanced and stubby rather than long and stretched, which is a strong clue to the -700 model.
The wingtip devices, if present, rise from a wing attached to a fuselage that looks notably shorter than the common 737-800.
The 737-700 does not have the chevron-edged engine nacelles seen on some newer Boeing twinjets, helping narrow the type.
In side view, it looks like a medium-length narrow-body jet that is shorter than the most common 737 versions but longer than the smallest one.
737-200: The Boeing 737-200 has short, stubby engine nacelles mounted directly under the wing with a noticeably low ground clearance.
Its engines are classic JT8D turbojets with circular inlets and no flattened bottom, unlike later 737 models.
The nacelles often look like narrow tubes or cigars rather than the larger fan-shaped pods seen on newer jets.
A 737-200 usually has a long, slender fuselage paired with relatively small engines that make the wing look dominant.
The nose gear sits low, giving the aircraft a slightly crouched stance on the ground.
The main landing gear does not retract into enclosed bays, so the wheels remain partly visible when retracted.
Its tail cone is long and pointed, especially on versions fitted with a rear airstair.
Many 737-200s have a gravel deflector on the nose gear, which appears as a prominent metal shield in front of the wheel.
The wing is simple and clean with no winglets on standard examples.
The cockpit windows have the classic early 737 shape, which looks less refined than on more modern airliners.
The fuselage is narrower and more compact-looking than later stretched 737 variants.
The aircraft often appears low-slung because both the fuselage and engines sit close to the ground.
The engine exhausts are narrow and prominent, extending clearly behind the wing trailing edge.
Its vertical tail is relatively tall and plain, without the blended styling cues seen on later generations.
The 737-200 has a short-to-medium body length that gives it a balanced, almost compact appearance.
From the side, the aircraft is easy to spot by the combination of tiny turbojet engines and a conventional narrow-body fuselage.
The underside of the wing and engine installation looks very simple, with little of the bulky fairing seen on modern designs.
On many examples, the nose section looks rounded and straightforward, matching the early-generation jetliner style.
The airplane lacks the large high-bypass engine look that characterizes later 737 Classics and Next Generation models.
A key recognition feature is the pairing of old-style skinny engines, no winglets, and partially exposed main wheels in flight.
737-800: The Boeing 737-800 has a noticeably longer fuselage than the 737-700 but is shorter than the 737-900.
It usually has four full-size passenger doors on each side plus overwing exits, a common clue for the -800 layout.
The wing sits low on the fuselage and carries engines that hang close to the ground.
Its engines have flattened lower nacelles, giving them a distinctly non-circular front shape.
The nose profile is the classic 737 shape with a relatively blunt, rounded appearance.
The main landing gear does not fully retract into covered bays, leaving the wheels partly visible when retracted.
The vertical tail is fairly tall and broad, matching the familiar Next Generation 737 family silhouette.
Most 737-800s have blended or split winglets, which are a common visual feature on this model.
The cockpit windows have the angular Boeing style rather than the more curved Airbus look.
The fuselage is narrow-body in width, with a single aisle and a slim cross section.
The wings are swept but not extremely long, giving the aircraft a compact and efficient appearance.
The tailcone is short and clean, without the extended tail skid fairing seen on some other jet types.
The nose landing gear sits relatively close to the cockpit, consistent with the short 737 nose section.
Compared with the 737-300 or 737-400, the 737-800 has a more modern wing and larger winglets.
The cabin window line is long and straight, reflecting the stretched single-aisle fuselage.
The aircraft often appears slightly nose-high when parked because of the 737’s low stance.
The engine nacelles sit ahead of the wing leading edge and look larger than those on earlier Classic 737s.
The tail and rear fuselage proportions give it a balanced look that differs from the shorter 737-700.
The overwing exit arrangement is a quick spotting feature because the 737-800 typically has two exits over each wing.
The overall impression is of a low-slung, narrow-body twinjet with classic 737 proportions and modern winglets.
757-200: The Boeing 757-200 has a long, narrow fuselage with a noticeably slender single-aisle body.
It has two turbofan engines mounted under the wings, one on each side.
The landing gear is relatively tall, giving the aircraft a high stance above the ground.
The nose gear sits far forward, creating a long stretch of fuselage between the main gear and the cockpit.
The wings are moderately swept and appear fairly large in relation to the narrow fuselage.
The vertical tail is tall and broad, giving the aircraft a strong upright profile.
The cockpit windows have the classic Boeing shape with angled side panes.
The aircraft usually has four main cabin doors on each side, with two forward and two aft of the wing.
Small overwing emergency exits are typically visible between the main doors.
The fuselage often looks especially long compared with other narrow-body airliners.
The engines appear relatively powerful and round, reflecting the type's strong performance.
The main landing gear has a simple twin-bogie arrangement with four wheels on each main gear leg.
From the side, the aircraft sits with a slightly nose-up appearance when on the ground.
The tailcone is clean and tapered, ending in a neat pointed rear fuselage shape.
The wings are mounted low on the fuselage in the standard airliner configuration.
The horizontal stabilizers are mounted low on the tail rather than in a T-tail arrangement.
The windows form a long straight row along the fuselage, emphasizing the aircraft's length.
The 757-200 has a distinctly taller and more stretched look than a 737.
Compared with a 767, it has only one aisle and a much narrower fuselage.
In profile, the combination of long body, tall gear, and large tail is a strong clue that it is a 757-200.
747-200: The aircraft has the classic Boeing 747 hump with a shorter upper deck than later stretched-upper-deck variants.
It has four turbofan engines mounted on pylons under a swept low wing.
The nose profile is the early 747 shape with a prominent cockpit section above the main deck.
The upper deck usually ends well before the wing root, giving the hump a compact appearance.
It has a very large widebody fuselage with a distinctive double-deck forward section only.
The main landing gear arrangement includes two body gear trucks and two wing gear trucks.
Each main landing gear truck has four wheels, creating a notably complex gear layout.
The vertical tail is tall and broad, matching the classic first-generation 747 silhouette.
The horizontal stabilizers are mounted low on the tail rather than in a T-tail configuration.
The wing has noticeable sweep and often shows wingtip fence-free, raked-free early 747 styling.
The 747-200 typically lacks the stretched upper deck seen on many 747-300 and 747-400 aircraft.
Many examples have older-style engine nacelles compared with newer 747 variants.
The cockpit windows have the unmistakable classic 747 arrangement with angled side glazing.
The nose landing gear sits far forward under the nose, emphasizing the aircraft’s long fuselage.
The fuselage side often shows a main-deck door layout typical of early 747 passenger or combi models.
The aircraft sits relatively low for its size because of the multi-bogey landing gear design.
It has a wide wingspan and thick inboard wing sections that give it a heavy long-haul appearance.
From the side, the aircraft looks like an early jumbo jet because of its short hump and simple wing tips.
Cargo versions can be identified by the upward-opening nose door while retaining the same basic 747-200 shape.
Overall, it appears as a first-generation jumbo jet with a short upper deck, four engines, and classic 1970s 747 proportions.
747-300: The 747-300 has a noticeably stretched upper deck compared with earlier 747 variants.
Its upper deck hump extends much farther forward and backward than on a 747-100 or 747-200.
The aircraft keeps the classic 747 nose shape with a prominent cockpit perched above the main deck.
It has four engines mounted under a swept low wing, matching the traditional 747 layout.
The fuselage is very long and wide, giving it the unmistakable jumbo jet appearance.
A long row of windows on the upper deck is a key clue that it is a 747-300.
The upper deck is shorter than on a 747-400 but clearly longer than on the earliest 747s.
Most 747-300s have winglets absent, which helps separate them from many 747-400 aircraft.
The tail is tall and conventional, with the large vertical fin typical of the 747 family.
The main landing gear consists of four bogies under the fuselage and wings, a classic 747 feature.
The stretched upper deck often makes the side profile look more balanced and less nose-heavy than earlier 747s.
From the side, the hump blends into the fuselage over a longer section than on older 747 variants.
It lacks the modern raked wingtips and other late-generation refinements seen on newer Boeing widebodies.
The cabin window pattern usually shows a distinct second-deck passenger section above the forward fuselage.
Compared with a 747SP, the 747-300 has a much longer fuselage and a less compact appearance.
Compared with a 747-400, the 747-300 usually looks cleaner at the wingtips because it often has no winglets.
The forward fuselage door and window arrangement reflects the extended upper deck passenger cabin.
Its overall silhouette is that of a classic 747 with the most obvious change being the long upper deck.
Seen head-on, it has the broad body and wide wing span of a heavy four-engine long-haul airliner.
The easiest recognition feature is the long upper deck without the more advanced external updates of later 747 models.
747-400: The aircraft has a very distinctive hump-shaped upper deck ahead of the wings.
The upper deck on a 747-400 is longer than on earlier 747 variants, with many windows stretching farther back.
It is a very large four-engine jet with two engines mounted under each wing.
The winglets at the wingtips are tall and clearly visible, unlike the earlier 747-100 and 747-200 models.
The fuselage is exceptionally wide and deep, giving the aircraft a bulky double-deck-front appearance.
The nose is rounded and blunt, with the cockpit windows set above the main deck contour.
The main landing gear is complex and heavy-looking, with multiple bogies under the fuselage and wings.
There is a small but noticeable upstairs cabin row of windows above the forward fuselage.
The tail is tall and broad, proportioned to match the very large fuselage.
From the side, the aircraft’s long fuselage and pronounced upper-deck hump make it easy to recognize.
The wings are swept and very large, with a broad span that suits a long-haul jumbo jet.
Each wing carries two large turbofan nacelles spaced evenly along the underside.
Compared with an Airbus A380, the second deck does not run the full length of the fuselage.
Compared with a 747-8, the 747-400 has shorter, less raked wingtips and a shorter upper deck profile.
The cockpit area has the classic 747 look, with windows appearing perched above the nose.
The wing roots blend into a deep fuselage, emphasizing the aircraft’s massive body size.
The aircraft usually sits relatively high off the ground because of its large landing gear and fuselage height.
Viewed head-on, the fuselage looks wide and rounded with four engines spread across a broad wing.
The 747-400 freighter version often has the same hump and winglets, plus a nose cargo door outline.
Its overall silhouette is defined by the combination of four engines, winglets, and the iconic forward hump.
747-100: The Boeing 747-100 has a short upper deck hump with only a small row of windows ahead of the wing.
It uses the early 747 upper deck that ends well before the wing root instead of the stretched upper deck seen on later models.
A 747-100 usually has three upper-deck windows per side, though some aircraft were later modified.
The aircraft has the classic four-engine 747 layout with one engine mounted under each wing section.
Its nose shows the original 747 cockpit perched above the main deck, creating the distinctive bulbous front profile.
The fuselage is very wide and deep, giving the airplane a massive cylindrical body compared with most airliners.
The tail is tall with a large swept vertical fin that looks proportionate to the original early 747 fuselage.
A 747-100 typically has the early-generation JT9D engine nacelles with a relatively simple, classic 1970s appearance.
The wings have no winglets on standard 747-100 aircraft, unlike some later 747 variants and retrofits.
The main landing gear consists of four body and wing gear assemblies plus the nose gear, a hallmark of the 747 family.
The upper deck on a 747-100 looks noticeably shorter than on a 747-300 or 747-400.
The side profile shows a long main deck with a small hump at the front, which is a key early 747 cue.
Many 747-100s have older-style cabin window and door arrangements that reflect the original baseline 747 layout.
The aircraft lacks the more modern wingtip extensions and aerodynamic refinements seen on later 747 versions.
From the front quarter view, the 747-100 appears chunky in the nose with the cockpit windows set high above the cargo door line.
The engine pylons and nacelles look more rounded and less refined than those on later 747 developments.
Its overall silhouette matches the original jumbo jet shape introduced at the start of the 747 family.
The short upper deck and absence of winglets together are among the quickest visual clues for a 747-100.
Compared with later 747s, the 747-100 often looks plainer externally because it lacks many later updates and fairing changes.
If the aircraft shows the original short hump, early engine style, and no winglets, it is likely a 747-100 or another early 747 variant.
737-900: The 737-900 has a noticeably longer fuselage than earlier 737 classics and NG variants like the 737-700 or 737-800.
It usually has four full-size main exit doors on each side instead of the overwing exit layout seen on many shorter 737s.
The cabin window line stretches much farther fore and aft because of the aircraft’s extended body length.
The wings and engines look similar in size to other 737 Next Generation models, making the extra fuselage length stand out.
The aircraft often appears slightly stretched and slender because the body is long while the landing gear remains relatively short.
The nose-to-wing distance and wing-to-tail distance both look extended compared with shorter 737 family members.
On many 737-900ER aircraft, there are additional mid-cabin exit doors that interrupt the window pattern.
The tail height is not dramatically larger than on a 737-800, so the fuselage can look unusually long relative to the tail.
The engine nacelles have the flattened-bottom 737 style, confirming it is a 737 rather than a different narrowbody type.
The main landing gear sits under a long fuselage, which can make the airplane look low to the ground when viewed from the side.
The winglets, if fitted, match 737 NG styling and help separate it from the newer 737 MAX family with different nacelles and details.
The cockpit windows and nose shape are standard 737 NG features, so identification often depends on judging the stretched fuselage.
The rear fuselage extends a long way behind the wing, more than on a 737-800, giving the jet a balanced but elongated profile.
The airplane lacks the distinctive taller landing gear and reshaped engine installation of the 737 MAX series.
Compared with an Airbus A321, the 737-900 has shorter landing gear, flatter-bottom engine nacelles, and a different nose profile.
The dorsal fin and vertical tail look typical for a 737 NG, which emphasizes that the body length is the main clue.
From a side view, the spacing of doors and windows reveals a long single-aisle cabin characteristic of the 737-900.
The wing sits relatively far forward on the long fuselage, leaving a substantial rear cabin section behind it.
If seen next to another 737 NG, the 737-900 is the one with the most stretched body while keeping nearly the same wing and tail proportions.
The overall impression is of the longest 737 Next Generation variant, with a long tube-like fuselage and familiar 737 NG details.
757-300: The 757-300 has a very long, stretched fuselage that looks noticeably longer than a 757-200.
Its body appears unusually slim and elongated compared with most single-aisle airliners.
The aircraft keeps the narrow-body 757 cross section despite having a length close to some wide-body jets.
It usually has four full-size passenger doors on each side, which helps identify the stretched variant.
The spacing between the doors is longer and more even because of the extended fuselage.
The wings look relatively small compared with the very long fuselage, giving it a distinctive proportions.
It has the same general nose shape as other 757s, paired with a much longer cabin section.
The landing gear sits far apart along the long fuselage, emphasizing the airplane's stretched look.
From the side, the tail seems set far behind the wing because of the added fuselage length.
The 757-300 often looks low and long, almost like a pencil with wings attached.
It has a tall vertical tail like other 757s, but the fuselage length makes the tail seem smaller in proportion.
The overwing exits are located between widely spaced main doors, helping separate it from shorter 757 models.
Compared with a 767, it has only one aisle and a much narrower fuselage, despite a similar overall length impression.
The engines are mounted under the wings like other 757s, but the extra-long fuselage is the key giveaway.
The nose gear sits relatively far forward with a long stretch of fuselage continuing behind the wing.
When viewed at the gate, the aircraft often occupies more terminal space lengthwise than expected for a narrow-body jet.
The cabin window line runs for a very long distance, making the airplane easy to recognize in profile.
It lacks the hump of a 747 and the wide fuselage of larger twins, yet still appears exceptionally long.
The tail cone and rear fuselage look standard for a 757, but they are attached to a much longer main body.
Among single-aisle airliners, the 757-300 stands out for its combination of great length, narrow width, and classic 757 nose and tail.
767-200: The 767-200 has a twin-engine widebody fuselage that looks wider than a 757 but shorter than most other 767 variants.
It usually has two large turbofan engines mounted under low swept wings, one on each side.
The fuselage is relatively short for a 767, giving it a compact widebody appearance.
It has the classic 767 nose shape with a smoothly rounded radome and slanted cockpit windows.
The main landing gear has two wheels on each side of each main strut rather than a larger multi-bogie arrangement.
Its wings are moderately swept and often appear long in relation to the short fuselage.
The tail is a conventional swept vertical fin with a low-mounted horizontal stabilizer.
From the side, the aircraft often shows four full-size passenger doors, two on each side of the fuselage.
Some examples have a noticeably shorter body than the more common 767-300, with less space between the wing and rear door.
The overwing area sits above a wide fuselage with two aisles inside, which can be inferred from the broad cross-section.
The wing roots blend into a wide center fuselage belly characteristic of a medium-size twin-aisle jet.

Spitfire: The wings have a smooth oval planform with rounded tips that is very distinctive in side and top views.

Tornado: A tornado often appears as a narrow, rotating funnel that extends from the base of a thunderstorm cloud toward the ground.
The funnel shape is usually tapered, with a wider top near the cloud and a narrower lower section.
Many tornadoes show a visible connection between a dark cloud base and the surface below.
A rotating column of dust, dirt, or debris at ground level can reveal a tornado even when the funnel is faint.
The cloud base above a tornado is often very dark and low compared with the surrounding sky.
Tornadoes commonly form beneath a large, rotating storm structure that looks organized and severe.
The funnel may look smooth and rope-like in weak tornadoes or thick and wedge-shaped in strong ones.
Rapid spinning motion in the funnel or debris cloud is a key visual sign of a tornado.
A tornado often appears nearly vertical, though some can be slightly tilted by storm winds.
Condensation in the funnel can make it look white, gray, or black depending on lighting and debris.
Debris being lifted and circling near the ground is a strong indicator of tornadic rotation.
A wedge tornado looks unusually wide, sometimes appearing broader than it is tall.
Some tornadoes are partially hidden by rain, but a concentrated rotating debris area can still mark their location.
The area around a tornado may show strong contrast between a bright sky region and a very dark storm core.
The funnel usually descends from a lowered, localized part of the storm base rather than from a flat cloud layer.
Multiple vortices may sometimes be visible as smaller rotating strands within or around the main tornado.
The surrounding storm can show curved cloud bands and a structured appearance that supports tornado identification.
A tornado’s lower end often interacts violently with the surface, producing a chaotic spray of dust and debris.
The condensation funnel may change shape quickly, stretching, narrowing, or thickening over short periods.
Unlike ordinary scud clouds, a tornado shows focused vertical rotation and a persistent connection to the storm base.
